name: BlazeDiff core-wasm (@blazediff/core-wasm)
workload: Pixel-by-pixel YIQ perceptual image diff of PNG fixtures (4K, ~1.6 MP and page-sized images, with identical-pair variants), decode excluded, 25 iterations after 5 warmup, Node.js.
claimed_speedup: ~50.8% faster on average than pixelmatch; 4k/1 332.26 ms vs 33.18 ms (90.0% less time, ~10x, derived from page data); 4k/3 423.14 ms vs 44.65 ms; small blazediff/1 1.24 ms vs 0.24 ms; identical-pair rows near parity (4k/2 identical 22.70 ms vs 22.17 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Rust, cargo build --release (opt-level 3, lto=true, codegen-units=1) for wasm32-unknown-unknown with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+simd128,+bulk-memory', wasm-bindgen 0.2.100 post-processing (crates/blazediff/scripts/build-wasm.sh); rustc version not stated.
hardware: Apple M1 Max, Node.js 22, macOS (BENCHMARKS.md 'Hardware Specifications')
tradeoffs: Needs WebAssembly SIMD (v128). Classifies pixels with the same YIQ delta as pixelmatch but not bit-identically: counts differ by up to ~0.05% (e.g. 22,869 vs 22,883 differing pixels). Part of a larger ecosystem (JS core, native Rust binary, PyPI bindings).
caveats: First-party benchmark, measured in Node.js on Apple Silicon, not in a browser. Pixelmatch's own times differ between the JS table (4k/1 201.60 ms) and the wasm table (332.26 ms), so absolute ratios shift run to run. Byte-identical pairs used to be a loss and are now only a small win. The README states a wasm-specific fix (skipping a scalar memcmp shortcut) was needed to turn the identical rows into wins.
found_via: npm registry search API (queries such as 'wasm simd fast', 'wasm faster than javascript', 'keywords:wasm'), README triage for 'Nx faster' claims; npm package @blazediff/core-wasm; opened repo README, BENCHMARKS.md, benchmarks/pixel-by-pixel.md and crates/blazediff/scripts/build-wasm.sh

name: TurboRes
baseline: FFmpeg 7.1.1 native CLI (single- and multithreaded, plus VideoToolbox hardware decode) and ffmpeg.wasm
workload: Apple ProRes decode (422 HQ 4K, 4444 1080p, 422 HQ 1080p, 422 Proxy 1080p), frames per second averaged over 10 runs of decoding a file.
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded: 42 FPS vs 15 FPS native FFmpeg at ProRes 422 HQ 4K (~2.8x, derived from page data), 128 vs 55 (4444 1080p), 158 vs 57 (422 HQ 1080p), 450 vs 161 (Proxy 1080p). Multithreaded: 250 FPS vs 107 FPS native FFmpeg and 84 FPS ffmpeg.wasm at 4K; 2310 vs 948 FPS at Proxy 1080p. Native hardware-accelerated FFmpeg: 160 FPS at 4K.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16: zig build-exe -target wasm32-freestanding -O ReleaseSmall -mcpu=generic+atomics+bulk_memory+multivalue+nontrapping_fptoint+reference_types+sign_ext+simd128 -fno-single-threaded (scripts/build-zig.sh --release); FFmpeg native build flags not stated.
hardware: Apple M4 (4P+6E) MacBook Air; TurboRes 1.2.0, FFmpeg 7.1.1
tradeoffs: Decoder only (no ProRes encoder). Needs WebAssembly SIMD; the multithreaded path uses wasm shared memory and a worker pool option. MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft. Hand-written for ProRes, so no other codecs.
caveats: First-party numbers on one Apple M4 laptop; FFmpeg is driven through its CLI and its build configuration is not stated, so process and output handling may be included in the native numbers. The release build uses ReleaseSmall. Benchmark scripts are in benchmark/ (benchmark-turbores.html, benchmark-ffmpeg-wasm.html, benchmark-ffmpeg-native.sh) so the table is reproducible, but the video files are hosted on an external bucket.

name: sh-syntax
baseline: mvdan-sh (GopherJS build of mvdan/sh, pure JavaScript)
workload: Formatting (print) of the shell script test/fixtures/install.sh with the same options through sh-syntax (TinyGo wasm) and mvdan-sh, measured with mitata under Node.
claimed_speedup: 18.33 ms/iter vs 79.47 ms/iter for mvdan-sh, 4.34x faster (summary line on page); synckit worker variant 18.38 ms.
compiler_and_flags: TinyGo: tinygo build -o main.wasm -target ./target.json --no-debug (package.json 'wasm' script); TinyGo version not stated. Benchmark source: benchmark/index.js (mitata).
hardware: Apple M1 Max (~2.81 GHz), node 18.20.8 arm64-darwin
tradeoffs: Wasm must be loaded asynchronously (fetch or bundler wasm?init) and uses Go's wasm_exec glue; the synckit variant is needed for a synchronous API in Node. Wraps mvdan/sh, so shell dialect support follows that project.
caveats: Single workload (one install script, format only), first-party, old Node 18 on Apple Silicon. The baseline is a GopherJS transpilation of the same Go parser, so the ratio compares wasm against transpiled JS of the same code, not against a hand-written JS shell parser.

name: MD4X (md4x)
baseline: markdown-it (JavaScript); also compared with its own native NAPI build
workload: Markdown to HTML (renderToHtml) on a medium fixture through md4x.wasm, md4x.napi, md4w, markdown-it, markdown-exit, satteri, ox-content and qip.wasm, measured with mitata under Bun.
claimed_speedup: md4x.wasm renderToHtml 15.08 us/iter vs markdown-it 72.68 us/iter (~4.8x, derived from page data); md4x.napi (native) 7.38 us, 9.85x faster than markdown-it and 2.05x faster than the wasm build; wasm is 17.40 us for md4w in the same table.
compiler_and_flags: Zig (a Zig port of mity/md4c); wasm and NAPI packages built with zig build wasm / napi-all at ReleaseFast (build.zig pkg_optimize); bench source packages/md4x/bench/index.mjs
tradeoffs: Version 0.0.x, so the API may still change. Ships both a native NAPI addon (about 2x faster than its wasm build in these numbers) and a wasm build for browsers and edge runtimes. CommonMark/GFM via md4c semantics.
caveats: First-party benchmark run under Bun, not in a browser. The bench file notes that options were aligned between libraries (e.g. GFM enabled for the others because ox-content defaults to off), but output equivalence across the parsers compared was not verified. Only the medium fixture is enabled in the checked-in script. Related project md4w (wasm build of md4c in C) appears in the same table.

hardware: Apple Silicon (exact chip not stated), Node 26 and Chromium 153 / Firefox 155 / WebKit (Safari 26.6)

caveats: Very new, first-party, chip model missing, benchmark package (packages/bench) is private to the workspace but present in the repo. The internals of the baseline JS implementation were not inspected. Speed-ups measured on Apple Silicon only.

name: go-re2 (wasilibs/go-re2)
baseline: Go standard library regexp (also measured against a cgo build of the same RE2)
workload: Go stdlib regexp microbenchmarks (Match, Find, Compile) and the wafbench CoreRuleSet/Coraza workload with POST payloads of 1 B to 100 kB, with RE2 compiled to WebAssembly and translated to Go by wasm2go.
claimed_speedup: WAF/POST/1000 15.399 ms vs 4.734 ms (-69.26%); POST/10000 150.65 ms vs 19.90 ms (-86.79%); POST/100000 1511.3 ms vs 171.7 ms (-88.64%); Match/Easy0i/1M 29,087,522 ns vs 42,975 ns (-99.85%, ~677x, derived from page data). cgo build is a further ~30% faster than the wasm build. Smaller inputs lose: Find 162.3 ns vs 1057.0 ns (+551%), POST/1 +18.18%, compiles roughly 4-6x slower.
hardware: GitHub Actions runner (4 procs, '-4' suffix), CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Drop-in for regexp but no *Reader APIs, invalid UTF-8 handled differently, and for small patterns or inputs the library is slower than the standard library (the README says to stay on regexp then). Works without cgo. Compile cost is high.
caveats: Numbers are one sample run on virtualised CI hardware (the README says relative numbers within a run are only somewhat informative); the baseline is the Go stdlib rather than the same library compiled natively, which is reported only through the cgo column. The default build translates the wasm to Go source with wasm2go rather than running a wasm VM.

name: blake3-jit
workload: BLAKE3 hashing of 96 B, 512 B, 1 KB, 32 KB and 1 MB inputs through blake3-jit (JavaScript with runtime-generated WASM SIMD) versus the native napi addon.
claimed_speedup: 96 B: 362 MB/s vs 149 MB/s (2.4x faster); 512 B: 748 vs 521 MB/s (1.4x); 1 KB: 811 vs 701 MB/s (1.2x); 32 KB: 1.36 vs 1.97 GB/s and 1 MB: 1.38 vs 2.06 GB/s (native wins).
tradeoffs: Faster than the native addon only for small inputs where FFI overhead dominates; native wins from tens of KB up. Generates wasm at runtime so there is no .wasm file to ship.
caveats: First-party, no hardware, Node version or harness stated on the page (tier C). The win is about call overhead, not hashing speed; large inputs favour native. Baseline is a different implementation (the Rust blake3 crate via napi), not the same code compiled natively.
